Netherlands Gas & Water Utilities Workers Hold Nationwide Strike, Disrupting Operations

AMSTERDAM, June 14 – Thousands of workers across the Netherlands’ gas and water utilities sector staged a nationwide strike on Friday, halting operations at key facilities and affecting supply management within the industry, union representatives and company officials said.

Employees from major industry firms including DutchGasNet, AquaDelta and Regional WaterWorks walked off the job early Friday morning, calling for improved wages, better working conditions and enhanced safety protocols. The industrial action, coordinated by the United Utilities Workers Union (UUWU), is the largest walkout in the sector in over a decade.

“After months of negotiations, our members have made it clear that their demands for safer workplaces and a fair wage increase cannot be ignored,” said UUWU spokesperson Jeroen van der Laan. “This strike is a last resort, but we will maintain our action until serious proposals are put forward by employers.”

The walkout led to the shutdown or reduced staffing of numerous gas distribution and water treatment sites, as well as maintenance and customer service departments. DutchGasNet, which operates distribution pipelines in the northern provinces, reported that up to 60% of its workforce joined the strike, causing the company to suspend planned maintenance and reduce staff presence at control centers.

AquaDelta, which manages water purification facilities in the south-west, said that while essential safety personnel remained onsite under minimum staffing agreements, routine operations had been “significantly impacted.” The company’s spokesperson, Marijke Smit, stated, “We are working to ensure all critical processes continue, but many regular functions have been slowed or temporarily paused.”

Similar disruptions were reported by Regional WaterWorks, which serves several urban areas in the central Netherlands. Company officials acknowledged delays in meter readings and non-urgent repairs, and said customer inquiries were facing response times of up to several days due to the reduced workforce.

Industry analysts said the strike underscored long-running tensions over staffing levels and investments in modernization. “The demands from workers reflect deeper challenges in the sector, including aging infrastructure and pressure to meet new environmental standards,” said Pieter Brouwer, an independent utilities consultant.

Negotiations between the union and the Gas & Water Utilities Employers Federation are ongoing. Both sides said they remained open to further talks but had not yet scheduled a new bargaining session. The UUWU said the strike would continue indefinitely until an agreement is reached.
